title.value: Goblin (Guardian: The Lonely and Great God)

logline: An immortal goblin cursed with a sword in his chest searches for his human bride, whose touch alone can grant him the death he seeks.

bollymeter.basis: Writer Kim Eun-sook's Daesang win and an 18.68% finale rating mark a high-water point for Korean cable fantasy; the score holds on rewatches.

seasons.review_body: Goblin set benchmarks that Korean cable fantasy has not comfortably cleared since. Writer Kim Eun-sook collected the Baeksang Daesang, Gong Yoo took Best Actor, and the finale drew 18.68% nationwide, ranking seventh in Korean cable history. The MyDramaList audience score of 8.8 across 167,000 users reflects sustained affection rather than opening-week hype. Critics clustered around three praise points: the mythology's internal consistency, the cinematography, and the Goblin-Grim Reaper double act that gave the show its unexpected comic register. Dissenting voices pointed to the female lead's agency being limited by the mythology's rules. The OST, particularly Stay With Me by Chanyeol and Punch, became a cultural artefact independent of the show.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body: Goblin's premiere aired December 2, 2016 on tvN and opened with debut cable ratings of 6.9 percent - exceptional for a first episode on the channel. Writer Kim Eun-sook had been the dominant force in Korean fantasy romance for a decade, and the premiere demonstrated why: it moved from the Goryeo dynasty to modern-day Canada without losing coherence, establishing the goblin mythology, the reincarnation structure, and Gong Yoo's specific charismatic physical register in a first episode that had a density most shows take multiple episodes to achieve. The Korea Times noted 'the depth of perspective looking at the life of the goblin that bears a bloody sword in his chest immerses the audience into the fantasy story.' The MyDramaList audience score of 8.8 from 167,000 users reflected sustained affection for a premiere that established the visual language - the buckwheat flower field portal sequence was identified as the episode's defining image - before the show had an audience to confirm it was working.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere opens in the Goryeo dynasty and arrives in modern-day Canada without losing coherence, establishing the goblin myth, the reincarnation structure, and Gong Yoo's charismatic physical presence all at once. Debut ratings hit 6.9% cable, impressive for a first episode.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Goblin opening a portal in a field of buckwheat flowers - the image that defined the show's visual identity before it had an audience.

critic_note.text: The depth of perspective looking at life of the goblin that bears a bloody sword in his chest immerses the audience into the fantasy story.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 7
episode_reviews.review_body: Goblin Episode 7 is the midpoint where the show demonstrated it had earned the emotional credibility its scale required. Kim Eun-sook's writing balanced two tones simultaneously in this episode that the show had been maintaining in separate registers since the premiere: the Goblin-Grim Reaper dynamic reached its most absurdist-comic peak at the same moment the goblin-bride mythology delivered its first genuinely painful plot consequence. The formal achievement was in keeping both registers active simultaneously rather than alternating them - the episode's comedy and its sorrow occupied the same scenes rather than consecutive sequences. The Grim Reaper's past identity, hinted at across the first six episodes in details small enough to be absorbed without emphasis, collided with the present in Episode 7 in a way the show trusted the audience to process without underscoring. The MyDramaList community identified this as the season's first episode that confirmed the mythology's internal consistency could support the emotional weight the show was asking it to bear.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The midpoint is where the show earns its emotional credibility: the Goblin-Grim Reaper dynamic reaches its most absurdist-comic peak while the goblin-bride mythology delivers its first genuinely painful twist. Both tones coexist here more elegantly than anywhere else in the run.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Grim Reaper's past colliding with the present in a detail so small the show trusts the audience to absorb it without underscoring.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 13
episode_reviews.review_body: Goblin Episode 13 aired January 14, 2017 on tvN and was the penultimate episode that became the series' emotional apex and the moment critics and audiences most consistently identified as the show's formal peak. The mythology's cost - the specific consequence the show's internal rules demanded of its leads - arrived in this episode as something unavoidable rather than dramatic, which was the correct register for a show that had spent twelve episodes establishing exactly what the rules meant. Writer Kim Eun-sook committed to the consequence without the reversal that similar fantasy dramas typically deployed to soften equivalent moments; the writing earned the emotional response it was asking for precisely because it did not protect the audience from what the mythology required. The scene that broke Twitter during the episode's original broadcast was identified by Korean press as the most widely discussed single scene from a tvN drama since the channel's prestige era began - the disappearance staged as something ordinary, in the middle of a street, without the cinematic framing that would have announced it as an event.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The penultimate episode is the emotional apex - the mythology's cost becomes unavoidable and the show commits to a consequence that lesser fantasy dramas would have reversed by episode's end. The writing earns the tears it is asking for.
episode_reviews.the_moment: A disappearance in the middle of an ordinary street - a scene that aired and broke Twitter before the episode had finished streaming.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 16
episode_reviews.review_body: Goblin's series finale aired January 21, 2017 and drew 18.68 percent nationwide, ranking seventh in Korean cable television history. Writer Kim Eun-sook resolved the mythology across multiple reincarnation timelines with a finality that respected both the show's supernatural premise and the human need for closure that the audience had been accumulating across sixteen episodes. The final meeting between the goblin and his bride was the scene the entire series had been constructed to earn, and the episode's received wisdom - that it was the rare fantasy finale that did not collapse under its own ambition - reflected how precisely Kim Eun-sook had calibrated the mythology's internal rules against the emotional register the finale required. Writer Kim Eun-sook won the Baeksang Daesang for the season; the finale's ratings record was the commercial validation of a critical consensus that the show had achieved what it set out to achieve. The MyDramaList community score of 8.8 from 167,000 users sustained that assessment over the years that followed.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale drew 18.68% nationwide and became the seventh highest-rated drama in Korean cable history. It resolves the mythology across multiple timelines with a finality that respects both the supernatural premise and the human need for closure - the rare fantasy finale that does not collapse under its own ambition.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final meeting between the goblin and his bride - the scene the entire series was constructed to earn.
